identity.author: John Davenant

scope.locus: De praedestinatione Cap. X Corvinus + Ultimum Prima/Secunda open.
scope.next_locus: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda cont. (Aug. De bono pers. 23; Vasquez grace=predestination knot; Patres ante Pelagium; triple-cord ratio).

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. X / Corvinus: Contra Tilen. p.148 — not ‘God does not give, therefore he never willed to give,’ but ‘he wills gifts only to the little and obedient’
english: Corvinus’s reply (Contra Tilenum, p. 148) is of no weight. It does not follow, he says, that because God does not give this man faith, perseverance, or salvation, therefore he never willed to give them—but rather this: God wills those gifts only to the little, to those who labor and do the Father’s will. So this man did not receive them because he was not such—namely by his own fault.
sections.latin: Nullius momenti est quod huic argumento respondetur a Corvino, Contra Tilen. pag. 148. Non sequitur, inquit, Deus huic non dat fidem aut perseverantiam aut salutem, Ergo non voluit ei dare fidem, perseverantiam aut salutem: sed hoc potius; Deus non vult dare praedicta dona nisi parvulis, laborantibus et voluntatem Patris facientibus. Ergo huic data haec dona non fuerunt, quia talis non fuit, culpa scilicet sua.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. X reply: question is predestinating will to do or not do — God gave Peter faith eternally willed; not giving Judas proves preterition/reprobation
english: I answer: Corvinus has plainly forgotten what is under dispute. The question is not God’s will under any notion, but God’s will as predestinating to do or not do. This consequence is best and firmest: God gave Peter faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore by predestinating will from eternity he willed to give him those goods. No less firm the reverse: God did not give Judas faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore he passed him by, did not predestine him, reprobated him, and would not affect him with such great goods.
sections.latin: Respondeo, Corvinum immemorem plane esse qua de re disputetur. Non enim quaestio est de voluntate Dei sub qualibet notione, sed de voluntate Dei praedestinantis aliquid facere aut non facere. Est autem optima et firmissima consequentia; Deus dedit fidem, perseverantiam, et vitam aeternam Petro, Ergo voluntate praedestinante ab aeterno voluit illi dare fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam. Et e contra non minus firma est illa: Deus non dedit Judae fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam: Ergo illum praeteriit, non praedestinavit, reprobavit, tantis bonis afficere noluit.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. X: Corvinus’s ‘only to the little and obedient’ fails — same question returns; if God willed humility for Judas as for Peter, both would have it
english: What Corvinus adds—that it only follows God wills those goods to the little and obedient, so Judas lacked them by his own fault—fails first: the same question returns about that littleness and obedience that was asked about faith and salvation. Why did God not give Judas the littleness and obedience he gave Peter? Had he willed to give alike to both, it would have stood alike in both. When God wills to plant humility or littleness in the human will, no free will resists—such a will is not resisted, because willing not to resist is worked in the man himself; the will resists no further once willing to resist is taken away.
sections.latin: Quod autem subjungit Corvinus, id solum sequi, Deum non velle dare praedicta bona nisi parvulis et obedientibus, atque idcirco non fuisse data Judae, quia sua culpa talis non fuit; primo non valet; quia eadem quaestio adhuc manet de hac parvitate et obedientia, quae mota fuit de fide et salute. Quaero enim cur Deus non dederit hanc parvitatem et obedientiam Judae quam dedit Petro. Si voluisset pariter dare utrique, in utroque pariter exstitisset. Nam Deo volenti bonam humilitatis aut parvitatis qualitatem indere humanae voluntati, nullum resistit hominis arbitrium: Tali equidem voluntati non resistitur, quia velle non resistere in ipso homine operatur: Non enim ultra resistit voluntas cui velle resistere sublatum est.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. X: suspending gifts on prior littleness is Pelagian unless littleness itself is God’s special gift — Orange canon 6; preparing littleness for one is electing
english: Next: those who hang these gifts on prior littleness, unless they admit that littleness itself is God’s special gift, fall into Pelagianism and hit Orange canon 6. If they do admit it, that is the same as granting God prepared and gave that littleness—on which faith and salvation hang—to one and not the other, and prepared and gave faith and salvation themselves; which is nothing other than electing one and reprobating the other.
sections.latin: Dein, qui haec dona Dei suspendunt ex parvitate praeeunte, nisi fateantur hanc ipsam parvitatem esse speciale donum Dei, in Pelagianismum incidunt, et incurrunt in Canonem 6. Concilii Arausicani: Si autem fateantur, perinde est concedere Deum praeparasse et donasse hanc parvitatem, unde fides et salus dependet, uni et non alteri, atque praeparasse et donasse ipsam fidem et salutem; quod nihil aliud est, quam unum elegisse, alterum reprobasse.

sections.title: Cap. X Arg. X close: reprobates lack saving grace because they are not what God requires — that itself proves antecedent rejection; Col. i. 12; no middle between election and reprobation
english: Finally Corvinus says saving grace is not given to the reprobate because by their fault they are not what God prerequires—and that itself proves they were antecedently rejected or passed by. For God has decreed to make all the elect such as he is wont to prerequire for laying hold of grace and glory (Col. i. 12). Those he has not made such, he has not elected; and since there is no middle between election and reprobation, he has reprobated them. After so many twists we must come back here: those not given the grace of faith, repentance, and perseverance we acknowledge as passed by in the ordination to everlasting life; those for whom these were prepared and given we confess as elect. And as some were mercifully elected to these goods before foresight of them as existing in them, so some were passed by and not predestined to receive such things before they were foreseen as finally lacking them.
sections.latin: Denique, quod dicit Corvinus, reprobis non dari gratiam salutiferam, quia sua culpa tales non sunt, quales Deus praerequirit, hoc ipsum arguit eos fuisse antecedenter rejectos sive praeteritos: Nam Deus decrevit omnes electos tales efficere, quales ad capessendum gratiam et gloriam ipse solet praerequirere, Coloss. i. 12. Quos ergo tales non effecit, eos non elegit; et quia non datur medium inter electionem et reprobationem, eosdem reprobavit. Post tot anfractus et gyros huc itaque redeamus oportet, ut quibus gratia fidei, poenitentiae et perseverantiae data non fuerit, eos in ordinatione ad vitam aeternam praeteritos agnoscamus; sicut e contra, eos quibus haec fuerunt praeparata et donata, electos confiteamur. Atque ut quidam electi fuerunt misericorditer ad haec bona ante praevisionem eorundem ut in illis existentium, ita quidam praeteriti fuerunt, et ad talia accipienda haud praedestinati, antequam praeviderentur ut talibus bonis finaliter carentes.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum open: absolute predestination/preterition from mere divine good pleasure is not Augustine’s private opinion but received by anti-Pelagian councils — against Arminius/Corvinus
english: We now propose our last argument: to show that this teaching—the predestination of some and preterition of others from the mere good pleasure of the divine will, with no prior regard to opposite human acts, good or evil—was not some private opinion of Augustine or his disciples, but received and approved by the councils held against Pelagius and the Semipelagians. We do this because Arminius, Corvinus, and the other innovators boldly claim our doctrine was approved in no council—not even those against Pelagius. Yet certain premises must first be laid down.
sections.latin: Ultimum nostrum argumentum jam proponemus, in quo conabimur ostendere hanc sententiam de praedestinatione quorundam, et praeteritione aliorum ex mero voluntatis Divinae beneplacito, absque omni praecedaneo respectu ad oppositos hominum actus, sive bonos sive malos, non fuisse singularem quandam Augustini aut discipulorum ejus opinionem, sed receptam et probatam ab illis Conciliis quae contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos fuerunt celebrata. Hoc idcirco faciendum putavimus, quia Arminius, Corvinus, reliquique novatores confidenter asserunt, doctrinam hanc nostram in nullo Concilio fuisse approbatam, ne quidem in iis quae contra Pelagium fuere habita. Huic tamen argumento quaedam sunt a nobis necessario praemittenda.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Prima: early anti-Pelagian councils did not expressly define absolute predestination — yet defined much that cannot stand if absolute gratuitous predestination is overturned; Faustus condemned
english: First we confess: the councils against Pelagius and the Semipelagians in Augustine’s time or the age just after his death—Diospolis, Milevis, Carthage, Orange, and others—did not expressly, directly, and particularly sanction absolute predestination or condemn foresight-election and reprobation. Yet we affirm that much defined in those councils cannot stand if absolute gratuitous predestination is overturned, or if that conditioned election and preterition is set up which Faustus, then others, and at last Arminius undertook to cultivate and defend. Add that Faustus’s books, which labor to fix conditioned election and explode the absolute, were condemned by the ancient church—clear from Gratian, Distinctio 15; the decree stands in the councils’ Tomus, sanctioned by Gelasius in a synod of seventy bishops. Hormisdas, asked about Faustus’s book, answers that catholic doctrine should be learned from Augustine and Prosper, not from Faustus.
sections.latin: Primo, fatemur, Concilia quae celebrata fuerunt contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos ipsius Augustini temporibus, aut saeculo ab obitu ejus proximo, qualia fuerunt Diospolitanum, Milevitanum, Carthaginense, Arausicanum, aliaque nonnulla, non expresse, directe et particulariter sanxisse doctrinam de absoluta praedestinatione, aut condemnasse opinionem contrariam de electione et reprobatione ex praevisione diversorum actuum in hominibus. Illud tamen affirmamus, in hisce Conciliis multa fuisse definita quae stare non possunt absoluta et gratuita praedestinatione eversa, aut posita illa conditionata electione et praeteritione quam Faustus, et post illum alii nonnulli, ac tandem Arminius excolendam et defendendam susceperunt. Huc accedit, Fausti libros in quibus conditionatam illam electionem operose stabilire conatur, et absolutam explodere, damnatos fuisse ab antiqua Ecclesia, ut ex Gratiano liquet, Distinct. 15. Decretum extat a Tom. Conciliorum, et sancitum fuit a Gelasio in Synodo septuaginta Episcoporum. Hormisda etiam de Fausti libro consultus respondet, Doctrinam Catholicam ex Augustino et Prospero, non item e Fausto, disci oportere.

sections.title: Cap. X Ultimum Secunda open: Orthodox predestination must be gathered from what they settled on Grace — Augustine: predestination is grace’s preparation; Vasquez: same question of grace and predestination
english: That conditioned predestination was chiefly in view is likely from this: Peter the Deacon and other eastern orthodox sent to Rome judged Faustus’s books especially to be anathematized because they were written against the sentence of predestination (De incarnatione et gratia, last chapter). Second: we can and must gather the Orthodox view of predestination from what they settled on Grace against the Pelagians and their remnants. For as Augustine says (De praedestinatione sanctorum 10), between grace and predestination this alone differs: predestination is grace’s preparation; grace itself is the gift. So anyone who teaches that Christ’s saving grace hangs on God’s absolute will, and is not given or denied according to men’s diverse operations, must—if he would be consistent—hold the same of predestination and preterition.
sections.latin: Atque inter caetera vel praecipue spectasse doctrinam hanc de conditionata praedestinatione, inde probabile est: quod Petrus Diaconus, aliique orthodoxi ex Oriente Romam missi, hoc nomine potissimum Fausti libros anathematizandos censuerunt, quod contra praedestinationis sententiam scripti essent, De incarn. et grat. cap. ultimo. Secundo dicimus, Nos et posse et debere colligere quae fuerit Orthodoxorum de praedestinatione sententia ex illis quae de Gratia contra Pelagianos et Pelagianorum reliquias statuerunt. Nam ut inquit Augustinus, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 10, inter gratiam et praedestinationem hoc tantum interest, quod praedestinatio sit gratiae praeparatio, gratia vero ipsa donatio. Si quis igitur doceat gratiam Christi salutiferam ex absoluta Dei voluntate dependere, et minime dari hominibus aut negari pro diversis illorum operationibus, is de praedestinatione et praeteritione, si sibi constare velit, idem statuat est necesse.
